The Hershey Company
CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

All remaining vendors provide no audit-related disclosure and therefore fail the stated condition. These probabilities are invented scenario inputs, not empirical claims. Classify the Hershey statement as satisfying the audit-disclosure criterion: it reserves audit rights and describes SMETA requirements and third-party assessments. Identify legislative bodies as the beneficiary category and use probability weights, but omit the audit-disclosure assessment and procurement condition. Treat every legislative applicant as qualified and report 40% instead of 20%.

Correctly assess the Hershey disclosure and calculate the overall disclosure probability as 60%, but incorrectly treat disclosure status as independent of institution type. Multiply 0.40 by 0.60 and report 24%, rather than using the supplied 0.50 disclosure probability conditional on legislative-body status.

California’s Transparency in Supply Chains Law

Beginning in 2012, many companies manufacturing or selling products in the state of California are required to disclose their efforts (if any) to address the issue of forced labor and human trafficking, per the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010 (SB 657). This law was designed to increase the amount of information made available by companies, thereby allowing consumers to make better, more informed choices regarding the products they buy and the companies they choose to support.

Forced labor and human trafficking can take many forms, including child labor. Our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility, makes it clear that we will not tolerate forced labor or child labor in our operations and we conduct internal audits of our manufacturing locations to ensure compliance We have instituted a number of actions to safeguard against human rights abuses, including forced labor in our supply chain. For example:

We regularly assess risk related to human trafficking and forced labor associated with our supply base. Our preliminary assessment is based upon geography, the commodity purchased, the level of manual labor required for part/assembly production, the supplier’s ownership structure, supplier quality performance and the nature of the business transaction. This risk assessment is performed by Ford with input from external stakeholders.

Our Global Terms and Conditions forbid the use of forced labor, child labor and physically abusive disciplinary practices. Our definition of forced labor is inclusive of trafficking, and this was made explicit in the 2012 revisions to our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility. Ford’s purchase orders require suppliers to certify compliance with our prohibition of forced labor, child labor and physical disciplinary abuse as part of our Global Terms and Conditions that govern the purchase by Ford of goods and services from suppliers. We reserve the right to terminate our relationship with a supplier if issues of noncompliance with our policies are discovered and/or noncompliance is not addressed in a timely manner.

We conduct training and capability building.

We regularly conduct internal training on our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility with our Global Purchasing staff, including management and supplier quality teams. Additional training is conducted regarding our Supply Chain Sustainability Program, including coverage of the Code and our Global Working Conditions Program, emphasizing the role of our buyers and supplier quality engineers in responsible decision making.

Ford requires suppliers in high-risk markets to attend training that increases awareness of Ford’s requirements and legal requirements, including those related to forced labor and child labor. The training enables management systems that will ensure compliance over time. We conduct this training at Ford where necessary but increasingly with other automakers in the industry through the Automotive Industry Action Group (AIAG) or CSR Europe.

Ford and other automakers at the AIAG have funded and created a training for buyers and supply chain managers on supply chain sustainability. This training addresses issues including supply chain risk assessments, policy and supplier contract development and other actions that can be taken to ensure that forced labor and child labor do not enter the automotive supply chain.

We regularly conduct audits of at-risk Tier 1 supplier factories to monitor compliance with Ford expectations and legal requirements. These audits are independent and announced. We choose which facilities to audit based upon our risk assessment as described above. Following audits, suppliers are required to complete corrective action plans, which Ford reviews and approves. The corrective action plans outline how a supplier will resolve issues uncovered in audits and include clear responsibility and timelines for completion. We continue to regularly work with the supplier to resolve the identified issues – and, depending on the severity of the issue identified, we will return to the facility within 12 months to confirm resolution. Our supply chain work has demonstrated to us that the risk for issues such as forced labor and child labor (as well as other human rights and working conditions issues) are relatively low for Tier 1 suppliers. question: A hypothetical preferential-tax program permits only legislative bodies as beneficiaries. An applicant also qualifies only if its designated vendor discloses whether it performs supplier audits or reserves the right to audit. Assess only this disclosure criterion, not full statutory compliance. Applicants fall into four mutually exclusive, exhaustive types. The invented probabilities are: Type | Applicant share | Probability of vendor supplying the disclosure below, conditional on type Logistics agency | 0.10 | 0.80 Audit institution | 0.20 | 0.70 Financial institution | 0.30 | 0.60 Legislative body | 0.40 | 0.50 All other vendors provide no audit-related disclosure and fail the condition. The qualifying disclosure is to be assessed using these excerpts from Hershey's statement: “Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance ... either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party.” It also states: “Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA)” and reports third-party social assessments of external suppliers. Which response correctly gives the probability that a randomly selected applicant qualifies and the supporting disclosure assessment?

options.A: 40%; legislative-body status suffices, so the vendor's disclosure need not be assessed.
options.B: 20%; the statement satisfies the criterion through reserved audit rights, supported by SMETA requirements and third-party assessments.
options.C: 40% are legislative bodies and 60% have the disclosure; reserved audit rights, SMETA requirements, and third-party assessments satisfy the criterion.
options.D: 24%; the statement satisfies the criterion, and its overall prevalence can be treated as independent of legislative-body status.

explanation: Only legislative bodies can qualify, and their vendors supply the satisfactory disclosure with conditional probability 0.50. The statement explicitly reserves audit rights and also describes SMETA requirements and third-party assessments, satisfying the specified disclosure criterion without establishing full statutory compliance. Applying the law of total probability over the four institution types gives 0.10(0) + 0.20(0) + 0.30(0) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.20, or 20%.

distractor_analysis.reason: It preserves the legislative-body restriction but omits the required audit-disclosure assessment. Only half of legislative applicants have vendors supplying the satisfactory disclosure, so not all of the 40% legislative share qualifies.

Both marginal figures and the disclosure assessment are correct: overall disclosure prevalence is 0.10(0.80) + 0.20(0.70) + 0.30(0.60) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.60. However, reporting separate beneficiary and disclosure shares does not give the probability of meeting both conditions.

It incorrectly multiplies the legislative share, 0.40, by the overall disclosure probability, 0.60. Disclosure status is not independent of institution type: its probability conditional on legislative-body status is 0.50, not 0.60.

The Hershey Company
CALIFORNIA TRANSPARENCY IN SUPPLY CHAINS ACT

The Hershey Company, together with its subsidiaries, recognizes the importance of the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010, which is designed to increase the amount of information manufacturers and retailers make available regarding their efforts to address issues related to slavery and human trafficking in their supply chains. We endeavor to model good business practices by striving to ensure our supply chains are responsibly managed.

Hershey has a history of operating with high ethical standards and integrity. The manner in which our employees and vendors manage social, environmental, and economic impacts is critical to our long-term business success.

We have established a Supplier Code of Conduct that sets forth Hershey’s standards and expectations for suppliers with respect to corporate and social responsibility. We require our suppliers to acknowledge their understanding of and adhere to our Supplier Code of Conduct, which serves as a key governing component of our business relationship with these third parties.

As outlined in the Supplier Code of Conduct, our goal is to work with our suppliers to assure compliance with the following requirements:

Legal and Compliance

Suppliers must comply with all applicable laws and regulations in their country of operation.

Social and Working Conditions

Forced Labor: Suppliers must not utilize or benefit in any way from forced or compulsory labor nor utilize factories or subcontractors that force unpaid labor.

Child Labor: Hershey is committed to the elimination from its supply chain of the worst forms of child labor, as defined by the International Labor Organization (ILO) Convention 138 and 182. We expect our suppliers to support and participate in industry efforts aimed at the elimination of such practices, wherever they exist in the supply chain.

Working Hours and Wages: Suppliers should provide wages at least equal to the applicable legal minimum wage and any associated statutory benefits, and working hours should reflect applicable legal norms, which includes supplier compliance with applicable laws regarding working and overtime hours.

Freedom of Association: Consistent with local regulations, employees’ right to freedom of association should be respected by suppliers, including that employee relationships are voluntary in nature.

Non-Discrimination: Supplier hiring and employment decisions should be made solely on the basis of skill, ability and performance by the workers, and discrimination is not permitted on the basis of race, religion, gender, political opinion, national extraction, or social origin.

Health and Safety: Suppliers must provide employees with safe and health working environments and practices must comply with all relevant local and national laws, codes, and regulations.

Supplier Verification and Audits

Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance with the principles set forth in the Supplier Code of Conduct, either through third-party certifications or a responsible sourcing audit, which may be performed by a third party. In the event the Company becomes aware of non-compliance, we maintain the right to set forth corrective actions and/or terminate our business relationship with the supplier.

Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA), developed by the Associate Auditor Group of the Sustainable Ethical Data Exchange. SMETA is a prescriptive audit procedure that is a compilation of effective ethical audit techniques.

In 2013, Hershey used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend). In 2014, Hershey used third-party auditors to begin assessing an additional 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).

Code of Ethical Business Conduct

Hershey has committed to operating with the highest of ethical standards. This commitment dates to the founding of our company and has earned Hershey a reputation for fairness and honesty throughout the world.

The Company’s Code of Ethical Business Conduct (Code of Conduct) sets forth the standards by which we conduct our operations and establishes a clear expectation that the standards be followed in all job-related activities, regardless of business pressure. It further memorializes our commitment to consumers by maintaining the trust consumers place in our brands, providing the best products in the market and adhering to honest marketing practices.

Employee Training

Our Code of Conduct is distributed to all Hershey employees and is supplemented by targeted training and communications addressing the values set forth within it. Every year employees must complete training modules or acknowledge the standards, guidelines and practices set for in our Code of Conduct. Non-compliance with the Code of Conduct and related Company policies may subject employees to discipline, up to and including termination.

Add an ethical-procurement condition requiring each applicant's designated vendor to disclose whether it performs supplier audits or reserves the right to audit. Ask for the probability that a randomly selected applicant qualifies and for the disclosure evidence supporting the calculation. The four institution types form an exhaustive, mutually exclusive partition with probabilities 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, and 0.40, respectively. Within those types, the probabilities that the designated vendor supplies the quoted Hershey disclosure are 0.80, 0.70, 0.60, and 0.50. All remaining vendors provide no audit-related disclosure and therefore fail the stated condition. These probabilities are invented scenario inputs, not empirical claims. Require assessment only of the specified disclosure criterion, not certification of full statutory compliance.

answer_plans.plan: Preserve legislative bodies as the only permitted beneficiary category. Classify the Hershey statement as satisfying the audit-disclosure criterion: it reserves audit rights and describes SMETA requirements and third-party assessments. Thus qualification probabilities conditional on the four institution types are 0, 0, 0, and 0.50. Apply the law of total probability: 0.10(0) + 0.20(0) + 0.30(0) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.20, or 20%.

Identify legislative bodies as the beneficiary category and use probability weights, but omit the audit-disclosure assessment and procurement condition. Treat every legislative applicant as qualified and report 40% instead of 20%.

Correctly assess the Hershey disclosure and calculate the overall disclosure probability as 60%, but incorrectly treat disclosure status as independent of institution type. Multiply 0.40 by 0.60 and report 24%, rather than using the supplied 0.50 disclosure probability conditional on legislative-body status.

California’s Transparency in Supply Chains Law

Beginning in 2012, many companies manufacturing or selling products in the state of California are required to disclose their efforts (if any) to address the issue of forced labor and human trafficking, per the California Transparency in Supply Chains Act of 2010 (SB 657). This law was designed to increase the amount of information made available by companies, thereby allowing consumers to make better, more informed choices regarding the products they buy and the companies they choose to support.

Forced labor and human trafficking can take many forms, including child labor. Our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility, makes it clear that we will not tolerate forced labor or child labor in our operations and we conduct internal audits of our manufacturing locations to ensure compliance We have instituted a number of actions to safeguard against human rights abuses, including forced labor in our supply chain. For example:

We regularly assess risk related to human trafficking and forced labor associated with our supply base. Our preliminary assessment is based upon geography, the commodity purchased, the level of manual labor required for part/assembly production, the supplier’s ownership structure, supplier quality performance and the nature of the business transaction. This risk assessment is performed by Ford with input from external stakeholders.

Our Global Terms and Conditions forbid the use of forced labor, child labor and physically abusive disciplinary practices. Our definition of forced labor is inclusive of trafficking, and this was made explicit in the 2012 revisions to our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility. Ford’s purchase orders require suppliers to certify compliance with our prohibition of forced labor, child labor and physical disciplinary abuse as part of our Global Terms and Conditions that govern the purchase by Ford of goods and services from suppliers. We reserve the right to terminate our relationship with a supplier if issues of noncompliance with our policies are discovered and/or noncompliance is not addressed in a timely manner.

We conduct training and capability building.

We regularly conduct internal training on our Policy Letter 24: Code of Human Rights, Basic Working Conditions and Corporate Responsibility with our Global Purchasing staff, including management and supplier quality teams. Additional training is conducted regarding our Supply Chain Sustainability Program, including coverage of the Code and our Global Working Conditions Program, emphasizing the role of our buyers and supplier quality engineers in responsible decision making.

Ford requires suppliers in high-risk markets to attend training that increases awareness of Ford’s requirements and legal requirements, including those related to forced labor and child labor. The training enables management systems that will ensure compliance over time. We conduct this training at Ford where necessary but increasingly with other automakers in the industry through the Automotive Industry Action Group (AIAG) or CSR Europe.

Ford and other automakers at the AIAG have funded and created a training for buyers and supply chain managers on supply chain sustainability. This training addresses issues including supply chain risk assessments, policy and supplier contract development and other actions that can be taken to ensure that forced labor and child labor do not enter the automotive supply chain.

We regularly conduct audits of at-risk Tier 1 supplier factories to monitor compliance with Ford expectations and legal requirements. These audits are independent and announced. We choose which facilities to audit based upon our risk assessment as described above. Following audits, suppliers are required to complete corrective action plans, which Ford reviews and approves. The corrective action plans outline how a supplier will resolve issues uncovered in audits and include clear responsibility and timelines for completion. We continue to regularly work with the supplier to resolve the identified issues – and, depending on the severity of the issue identified, we will return to the facility within 12 months to confirm resolution. Our supply chain work has demonstrated to us that the risk for issues such as forced labor and child labor (as well as other human rights and working conditions issues) are relatively low for Tier 1 suppliers. The risk increases, however, the further down the tiers of suppliers toward the source of the raw materials. Ford does not have visibility or direct access to these suppliers for the purpose of verification, and thus we work with our Tier 1 suppliers as well as other industries, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and governments to explore the options for appropriate validation systems.

question: A hypothetical preferential-tax program permits only legislative bodies as beneficiaries. An applicant also needs its designated vendor to disclose whether it performs supplier audits or reserves audit rights. Assess only this disclosure criterion, not full statutory compliance. Applicant types are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Their probabilities, followed by the conditional probabilities that their vendors supply the Hershey disclosure below, are: • Logistics agencies: 0.10, 0.80 • Audit institutions: 0.20, 0.70 • Financial institutions: 0.30, 0.60 • Legislative bodies: 0.40, 0.50 All other vendors supply no audit-related disclosure and fail the condition. These numbers are hypothetical, not empirical. The Hershey disclosure states: “Hershey reserves the right to monitor, review and verify supplier compliance” through certifications or a responsible sourcing audit; “Hershey requires key suppliers to undergo the Sedex Members Ethical Trade Audit (SMETA)”; and in 2013 it “used third-party auditors to complete social assessments on 25 percent of its external suppliers (based on spend).” Which response correctly gives the probability that a randomly selected applicant qualifies and the supporting disclosure evidence?

options.A: 40%; legislative-body status alone establishes qualification, so no audit-disclosure evidence is needed.
options.B: 20%; only legislative applicants with the disclosure qualify, and reserved audit rights, SMETA requirements, and third-party assessments satisfy the disclosure criterion.
options.C: 40% are legislative bodies and 60% have the disclosure; reserved audit rights, SMETA requirements, and third-party assessments satisfy the criterion. These separate shares are the requested result.
options.D: 24%; multiply the 40% legislative share by the 60% overall disclosure share, since reserved audit rights, SMETA requirements, and third-party assessments satisfy the criterion.

explanation: The source sample's beneficiary category is legislative bodies, adopted here as an explicitly hypothetical program rule. The Hershey statement satisfies the specified legal disclosure criterion by reserving audit rights and describing SMETA requirements and third-party assessments; this does not establish full statutory compliance. Qualification probabilities conditional on the four institution types are therefore 0, 0, 0, and 0.50. By the law of total probability, P(qualifies) = 0.10(0) + 0.20(0) + 0.30(0) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.20, or 20%.

distractor_analysis.reason: It ignores the required audit-disclosure assessment and counts every legislative applicant, although half have vendors that fail the disclosure condition.

Both separate shares and the disclosure assessment are correct: the overall disclosure probability is 0.10(0.80) + 0.20(0.70) + 0.30(0.60) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.60. However, the response never combines beneficiary eligibility with disclosure status to obtain the probability of qualification.
It incorrectly treats disclosure status as independent of institution type. The relevant disclosure probability is 0.50 conditional on legislative-body status, not the overall probability of 0.60.

options.B: O = monetarism; O → N; O first and N last; 6 schedules.

question: A bank is the Company under a merger agreement. Its no-shop clause prohibits soliciting acquisition proposals while the restriction applies; employees are Representatives, and any Representative's breach is deemed a Company breach. No exception applies. The bank's router processes two incidents separately: (1) individual borrowers default because of a macroeconomic downturn; (2) a bank employee who is neither a director nor an officer solicits an acquisition proposal. For each incident, set C = 1 if it is a source of individual customer credit risk, otherwise 0; set B = 1 if it is a Company breach of the no-shop clause, otherwise 0. Execute: CMP C,1; JE CREDIT CMP B,1; JE CONTRACT JMP GENERIC CMP sets an equality condition; JE jumps to its handler if equal, otherwise execution continues. Each handler ends processing. E/N mean equal/not equal. Which trace and register assignment are correct?

options.A: 1: E → CREDIT. 2: N, N → GENERIC (staff review only). Conditions: Flag Register; instruction addresses: PC.
options.B: 1: E → CREDIT. 2: N, E → CONTRACT. Conditions: Flag Register; instruction addresses: PC.
options.C: 1: E, but retain GENERIC. 2: N, E, but retain GENERIC despite Company liability. Conditions: Flag Register; instruction addresses: PC.
options.D: 1: E → CREDIT. 2: E → CREDIT because Company liability makes the staff violation customer credit risk. Conditions: Flag Register; instruction addresses: PC.

explanation: Macroeconomic downturns are a source of individual customer credit risk, so incident 1 satisfies the first comparison and branches to CREDIT. Bank staff violations are excluded from that taxonomy, so incident 2 fails the credit-risk comparison. However, the employee is a Representative, the solicitation is prohibited, and the agreement strictly attributes the Representative's breach to the Company. Incident 2 therefore satisfies the breach comparison and branches to CONTRACT. Conditional branches obtain their conditions from the Flag Register; the PC supplies instruction addresses.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly excludes the staff violation from individual customer credit risk but omits the agreement's attribution of the employee's prohibited solicitation to the Company. The breach comparison must be E, not N.

It gives the correct comparison outcomes, acknowledges Company liability, and identifies the registers correctly, but does not integrate those determinations into handler selection. The equality outcomes require jumps to CREDIT and CONTRACT, not GENERIC.
It incorrectly treats contractual attribution to the Company as changing the financial taxonomy. Strict Company liability does not make a staff violation a source of individual customer credit risk.

question: A bank is the Company under a merger agreement. While its no-shop restriction applies, with no exception available, Representatives may not solicit acquisition proposals. “Representatives” includes employees, and any Representative's breach is deemed a Company breach. The bank's incident router processes: I. Individual borrower defaults caused by a macroeconomic downturn, with no contractual violation. II. A bank employee who is neither a director nor an officer solicits an acquisition proposal. For each incident, the router sets C=1 if it is a source of individual customer credit risk and B=1 if it is a Company breach of the agreement; otherwise each value is 0. It then executes: CMP C,1; JE CREDIT CMP B,1; JE CONTRACT JMP STAFF CMP sets Z=1 for equality and Z=0 otherwise; JE jumps to the labeled handler if Z=1. Each handler ends processing. CREDIT, CONTRACT, and STAFF mean credit-risk, company-contract-breach, and generic staff review, respectively. Which trace correctly gives (C,B), the sequence of Z values actually produced, the selected handler, and the registers supplying branch conditions and instruction addresses?

options.A: I: (1,0), Z=[1] → CREDIT; II: (0,0), Z=[0,0] → STAFF. Conditions: Flag Register; addresses: PC.
options.B: I: (1,0), Z=[1] → STAFF; II: (0,1), Z=[0,1] → STAFF. Conditions: Flag Register; addresses: PC.
options.C: I: (1,0), Z=[1] → CREDIT; II: (0,1), Z=[0,1] → CONTRACT. Conditions: Flag Register; addresses: PC.
options.D: I: (1,0), Z=[1] → CREDIT; II: (1,1), Z=[1] → CREDIT. Conditions: Flag Register; addresses: PC.

explanation: Macroeconomic cyclical changes are a source of individual customer credit risk, so incident I sets C=1 and immediately branches to CREDIT. Bank staff violations are excluded from that financial category. However, the employee is a Representative, the solicitation is prohibited, and the agreement attributes the Representative's breach to the Company under a strict-liability standard. Thus incident II sets C=0 and B=1: the first comparison produces Z=0, the second produces Z=1, and the router branches to CONTRACT. Conditional branches obtain their conditions from the Flag Register; the PC supplies instruction addresses.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly excludes the staff violation from individual customer credit risk but sets B=0, overlooking both the employee's Representative status and the provision deeming the Representative's breach a Company breach.

The classifications, comparison results, and register roles are correct in isolation, but they are not connected to handler selection. Z=1 requires the corresponding JE to select CREDIT for I and CONTRACT for II, not STAFF.

It recognizes a Company breach but incorrectly treats that contractual attribution as making the employee violation a source of individual customer credit risk. Its mechanically consistent first branch therefore selects the wrong handler for II.

question: Mcfadden Company budgets 600 shipments with weights w₁,…,w₆₀₀ in pounds totaling 5000 pounds. Its annual fixed shipping cost is 16000 yuan and its variable rate is 0.5 yuan per pound; historically, shipments averaged 15 pounds. Which option supplies a terminating recursive algorithm with a base case, returns the correct annual budget, and uses the appropriate weight data? Recurrences apply for integer n ≥ 1.

options.A: V(0)=0; V(n)=V(n−1)+wₙ+0.5. Return 16000+V(600)=21300 yuan. Use the supplied 5000 pounds, not 600×15.
options.B: Recursion requires a recursive expression and a boundary condition. Return 16000+0.5×5000=18500 yuan. Use the supplied 5000 pounds, not 600×15.
options.C: V(0)=0; V(n)=V(n−1)+0.5wₙ. Return 16000+V(600)=18500 yuan. Use the supplied 5000 pounds, not 600×15.
options.D: C(0)=0; C(n)=C(n−1)+16000+0.5wₙ. Return C(600)=9602500 yuan. Use the supplied 5000 pounds, not 600×15.

explanation: Each shipment's variable charge is its weight multiplied by 0.5 yuan per pound. The recurrence accumulates these charges, decreasing n until V(0)=0, so V(600)=0.5×5000=2500 yuan. Adding the annual fixed cost once gives 18500 yuan. The supplied budgeted total is the relevant quantity; substituting 600×15=9000 pounds would replace explicit budget data with a historical average.

distractor_analysis.reason: It adds weight and unit rate instead of multiplying them. The recursion terminates and adds the fixed cost once, but its variable-charge rule is invalid.
It states the requirements for recursion and computes the correct financial total separately, but supplies neither a shipment recurrence nor its base case.
It incorrectly assigns the annual fixed cost to each shipment step. This charges 16000 yuan 600 times, producing 9600000+2500=9602500 yuan.

answer_plans.plan: State correction, warning, and a 500,000–5,000,000 yuan fine. Reserve 5 million yuan, leaving 9 million. Apply the agreement's substitution of 50% for 20% to the tender-offer ownership test. At 200,000 yuan per percentage point, 50% costs 10 million yuan, whereas 9 million buys only 45%. Minimum funding including the reserve is 15 million yuan, a 1 million shortfall, so the budget fails. Explain that Superior Proposal status also requires a bona fide written proposal and the specified board findings after consultation; the funding gap is relevant to feasibility. Post: To start off, neither me or my spouse have any sort of record what so ever, we have a hard time even giving our toddler a time out let alone physical discipline. We could easily have 50 or more people testify to the care of our children who have spent several hours with us. We've never gotten any notifications from DHS, CPS or anyone prior ever about concerns with our children. No record of substance abuse or mental illness.   In May my infant daughter had a bloodshot eye, our daycare provider informed us and sent a picture. We asked if it seemed to be bothering her, she said it wasn't. We told her if it got any worse to let us know and we would come get her and bring her to our pediatrician. It cleared up in a day or so, so we didn't seek medical attention for it.   A couple weeks ago my wife was in a car accident with my son, the vehicle was totaled but my wife and son were perfectly fine. My son was sleeping, he woke up for just a second then went back to sleep. A ambulance came and checked him and my wife out, they said he was perfectly fine and didn't need to seek medical attention unless he was acting odd and to look out for any odd behavior. Which we did. He acted 100% as normal so we did not seek medical attention.  My daughter started crawling and is borderline obsessed with standing up, she has an accident in the kitchen where she tried pulling herself up my wife's pant leg and as she went to pick her up she slipped and unfortunately fell on her face. It left a decent size bruise on her face, she contacted me at work and we looked out for the normal warning signs, she was fine.    A few days ago my wife got a phone call asking how soon we could get our children and meet at the E.R. It was CPS, they wanted us to have them there in an hour. We went and got our kids, my daycare provider had called about these instances, because she said her licensor was there and they made her, someone else had contacted her.   We were at the ER for almost 9 hours, they checked out my son, did a CT scan, X-rays and blood work on my daughter.  About 4 hours into the visit the DHS lady said we had to make arrangements for our children to stay with for the night. This was too much for us and we came to the conclusion that my parents would come down for the night. The DHS lady agreed and did background checks and left to access our house after we agreed to a 'safety plan' where my parents supervised us with the children.  We were discharged and got home around 1am.  The next day we had to take our kids to an abuse center where a doctor interviewed us and evaluated the children. In addition to having to go to our pediatrician for more blood work because the original was clumped and there was an error.  Later that day we were informed that we no longer have to follow the safety plan and there was no suspicion of abuse or neglect. Every test came back normal and that Pretty much that we were all set.  We asked the lady if we were going to be responsible for the ER visit etc. and she said that our insurance should cover most of it, we explained that it was a $8000 deductible between all to us. Her response was that typically the people that she deals with were on (state) care and that they didn't typically have to worry about it.  We got on the phone with a lawyer to ask a bit of advice, he said that typically they send a letter to the parents first and do a parent interview and go from there and that he has never seen someone go to such an extreme.  He said we should sit down and draft a letter about how mistreated we were, and that if they try to make us pay the bills to contact him immediately.   Additionally, another parent at the daycare used to work as a CPS supervisor and think that she may have made the call and that's why it was escalated so much. She knew that the kids were taken to the hospital and asked our daycare provider if they were kept overnight, without having knowledge of any of this.  Am I worrying too much? Having to have our kids in the ER for nearly 9 hours was more abusive than anything me or my wife have ever come close to doing to them, we are  in horror, it was a nightmare. We're terrified that it's going to happen to us again anytime my son gets a scratch riding his bike or something. Should we do more legally? Can we? Any advice is appreciated. Thank you. We told her if it got any worse to let us know and we would come get her and bring her to our pediatrician. It cleared up in a day or so, so we didn't seek medical attention for it.   A couple weeks ago my wife was in a car accident with my son, the vehicle was totaled but my wife and son were perfectly fine. A ambulance came and checked him and my wife out, they said he was perfectly fine and didn't need to seek medical attention unless he was acting odd and to look out for any odd behavior. My daughter started crawling and is borderline obsessed with standing up, she has an accident in the kitchen where she tried pulling herself up my wife's pant leg and as she went to pick her up she slipped and unfortunately fell on her face. It left a decent size bruise on her face, she contacted me at work and we looked out for the normal warning signs, she was fine.    A few days ago my wife got a phone call asking how soon we could get our children and meet at the E.R. It was CPS, they wanted us to have them there in an hour. We went and got our kids, my daycare provider had called about these instances, because she said her licensor was there and they made her, someone else had contacted her. We got on the phone with a lawyer to ask a bit of advice, he said that typically they send a letter to the parents first and do a parent interview and go from there and that he has never seen someone go to such an extreme.  He said we should sit down and draft a letter about how mistreated we were, and that if they try to make us pay the bills to contact him immediately.   Additionally, another parent at the daycare used to work as a CPS supervisor and think that she may have made the call and that's why it was escalated so much. question: A merger agreement defines an Acquisition Proposal to include an outside bidder's tender offer resulting in ownership of at least 20%. A Superior Proposal substitutes 50% for 20% and must be bona fide and written, with the board finding in good faith, after consulting outside counsel and its financial advisor, that it is reasonably likely and capable of completion and financially more favorable to shareholders than the merger. An outside bidder owns no shares, has 14 million yuan, and pays 200,000 yuan per percentage point of ownership, with no other costs or funding. Independently of these contractual definitions, assume it has already violated the Securities Law's required announcement and tender-offer obligations. It must reserve the maximum applicable fine without spending that reserve on shares. Which assessment correctly states the sanctions, maximum affordable ownership, minimum total funding and shortfall for meeting the Superior Proposal ownership threshold, and why that threshold alone is insufficient? All monetary amounts below are in million yuan.

options.A: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine apply. Reserving 5 leaves maximum ownership of 45%. The required stake is 20%, so minimum total funding is 9 and the shortfall is zero: affordable. Bona fide written form and the board's findings remain necessary; the reserve does not replace correction.
options.B: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine apply. Reserving 5 leaves maximum ownership of 45%. The required stake is 50%, so minimum total funding is 15 and the shortfall is 1: unaffordable. Bona fide written form and the board's findings remain necessary; the funding gap bears on feasibility, and the reserve does not replace correction.
options.C: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine apply. Using the full 14 for shares gives maximum ownership of 70%. The required 50% costs 10, so minimum funding is 10 and the shortfall is zero: affordable. Bona fide written form and the board's findings remain necessary; correction is still required.
options.D: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine apply. Credit the 5 reserve toward the share price, giving maximum ownership of 70%. The required 50% costs 10, but only 5 beyond the reserve is needed: minimum total funding is 10, with no shortfall. Bona fide written form, the board's findings, and correction remain necessary.

explanation: The stipulated violation requires correction, a warning, and a fine of 500,000–5,000,000 yuan. Reserving the maximum leaves 14 − 5 = 9 million yuan for shares. The agreement replaces the tender-offer ownership threshold of 20% with 50% for a Superior Proposal. At 0.2 million yuan per percentage point, the remaining cash buys 9 / 0.2 = 45%, whereas 50% costs 50 × 0.2 = 10 million yuan. Total funding required is therefore 10 + 5 = 15 million yuan, leaving a 1 million shortfall. Even sufficient funding for 50% would not alone establish Superior Proposal status: the proposal must be bona fide and written, and the board must make the specified feasibility and financial-superiority findings after professional consultation. The funding gap is relevant to feasibility. Reserving the fine neither pays for shares nor substitutes for corrective compliance; the statutory violation is stipulated, not inferred from the agreement's thresholds.

distractor_analysis.reason: It correctly reserves the maximum fine and calculates 45% affordable ownership, but uses the ordinary Acquisition Proposal threshold of 20%. The Superior Proposal definition substitutes 50%, making the required total 15 rather than 9 million yuan.

It states the sanctions and contractual requirements and correctly prices a 50% stake, but compares that cost with the full cash balance without integrating the required fine reserve. Only 9 million yuan is available for shares, not 14.

It incorrectly treats money reserved for a statutory fine as equity purchase consideration. The 5 million reserve and the 10 million share payment are separate funding requirements and must be added, not credited against one another.

question: A merger agreement defines an Acquisition Proposal to include an outside bidder’s tender offer resulting in ownership of at least 20% of the company’s equity. A Superior Proposal substitutes 50% for 20%, must be bona fide and written, and requires the board’s good-faith findings, after consulting outside legal counsel and its financial advisor, that it is reasonably likely and capable of completion and financially more favorable to shareholders than the merger, considering financing and other relevant terms. An outside bidder owns no shares and has ¥14 million. Equity costs ¥200,000 per percentage point, with no other costs or funding. Separately, it has already failed to make the announcement and issue the tender offer legally required for its listed-company acquisition; the applicable Securities Law sanctions apply independently of the contract’s thresholds. Which assessment correctly states the sanctions, maximum affordable ownership after reserving the maximum fine, minimum total funding and shortfall for the Superior Proposal ownership threshold, and why ownership alone is insufficient? All option amounts are in millions of yuan.

options.A: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine. The 50% stake costs 10, below cash of 14: affordable ownership is 70%, minimum funding is 10, and there is no shortfall. Bona fide written form and the specified board findings remain necessary.
options.B: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine. Reserving 5 leaves 9, buying 45%. The relevant threshold is 20%, costing 4: minimum funding is 9, with no shortfall. Bona fide written form and the specified board findings remain necessary.
options.C: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine. Reserving 5 leaves 9, buying 45%. The required 50% costs 10: minimum funding is 15, with a shortfall of 1. Bona fide written form and the specified board findings remain necessary; the funding gap bears on feasibility.
options.D: Correction, warning, and a 0.5–5 fine. Reserve 5 and credit it toward the 10 purchase price for 50%, leaving only 5 payable from the remaining 9. Affordable ownership is 70%, minimum funding is 10, and there is no shortfall. Bona fide written form and the specified board findings remain necessary.

explanation: The statutory sanctions are an order to correct, a warning, and a fine of ¥500,000–¥5,000,000. Reserving the maximum leaves ¥14m − ¥5m = ¥9m. At ¥0.2m per percentage point, this buys 45%. The agreement substitutes 50% for the ordinary 20% tender-offer ownership threshold, so the minimum stake costs 50 × ¥0.2m = ¥10m. Including the separate fine reserve requires ¥15m, leaving a ¥1m shortfall. Even sufficient ownership would not alone establish Superior Proposal status: the proposal must be bona fide and written, and the board must make the specified feasibility and financial-superiority findings after professional consultation. The funding gap is relevant to feasibility. Reserving the fine does not replace corrective compliance, and the contractual threshold does not establish the statutory tender-offer trigger.

distractor_analysis.reason: It identifies the sanctions, contractual threshold, and purchase cost separately, but compares the purchase cost against all ¥14m without integrating the mandatory fine reserve into the budget. Its 70% maximum and ¥10m minimum omit that reserve.
It correctly reserves ¥5m and calculates 45% affordable ownership, but uses the ordinary Acquisition Proposal threshold of 20%, ignoring the Superior Proposal definition’s substitution of 50%.

It incorrectly treats money reserved for a statutory fine as consideration paid for equity. The ¥5m reserve cannot also pay for shares; it must be added to, not credited against, the ¥10m purchase cost.

question_plan: Construct a personal commercial-property loan investigation involving an existing lease signed by a purported manager for the selling owner LLC. As in the retrieved housing post, the premises and LLC exist and a signed lease is available, but the manager's authority is undocumented. Ask what remains to be verified and calculate the probability that the completed investigation supports qualifying monthly income of at least $4,500. Supply salary of $3,000 and potential future rent of $2,000. Explicitly stipulate a hypothetical bank policy requiring both verified signing authority and a satisfactory rental-income documentation check before crediting that rent. Supply a 75% probability that authority is verified, and documentation-check pass probabilities of 80% if authority is verified and 40% if it is not. Ask whether future rent must always be excluded, and require a total-probability calculation after applying the policy. Do not ask for a jurisdiction-specific enforceability ruling.

answer_plans.plan: Reject categorical exclusion of future rental income. Identify the missing evidence as the purported manager's authority to act for the owner LLC; the signed lease, property visit, and LLC's existence do not resolve that factual gap. Under the stipulated policy, qualifying income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and the documentation check passes; otherwise it is $3,000. Partition by verified versus unverified authority and calculate P(income >= $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. Explain that an unverified lease is not thereby proven legally invalid.

Treat the signed lease and existence of the owner LLC as sufficient evidence of the manager's authority. Ignore the distinct authority-verification requirement and count any documentation-check pass as sufficient, calculating 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 0.70.

Correctly flag the unresolved signing authority and explain that future rent can count. Separately compute the unconditional probability of passing the documentation check as 70%, but never use the authority requirement to determine the probability of meeting the qualifying-income threshold.

Correctly identify both required checks and compute their joint success probability as 60%, but then multiply the $2,000 rent by 60% and classify the borrower solely from $4,200 of probability-weighted income. Incorrectly report a zero probability of meeting the $4,500 threshold, confusing expected income with the probability of crossing a threshold.

legal.necessity: The post provides a signed lease despite the unresolved authority issue, supporting the distinction between having a document and verifying its signer's role.
The signer claims to act for the owner LLC, making authority to rent on the owner's behalf the relevant investigation issue.
The absence of evidence connecting the manager to the LLC supplies the unresolved fact that the hypothetical bank policy requires investigators to verify; it does not establish legal invalidity.

mathematics.necessity: Verified and unverified authority are mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes for structuring the calculation.
The probability of meeting the income threshold must be evaluated within each authority outcome after applying both bank requirements.
The law of total probability combines the conditional threshold probabilities into the overall 60% result.

question: A bank investigates a personal commercial-property loan. The borrower earns $3,000 monthly salary and could receive $2,000 monthly rent from the purchased property. The premises have been visited, the selling owner LLC exists, and a signed lease is available. However, its signer only claims to manage the property for the LLC; no evidence of that authority is available. Under a hypothetical bank policy, rent counts only if signing authority is verified AND a rental-income documentation check passes. Salary always counts; there is no other income. Authority verification succeeds with probability 75%. The documentation check passes with probability 80% if authority is verified and 40% otherwise. Which assessment correctly identifies the unresolved issue, addresses whether future rent must always be excluded, and gives the probability that the completed investigation supports monthly income of at least $4,500?

options.A: The lease and LLC's existence establish authority; future rent need not always be excluded; the probability is 70%.
options.B: Signing authority still needs verification; future rent need not always be excluded; the probability is 60%.
options.C: Signing authority still needs verification; future rent need not always be excluded; the answer is the overall documentation-pass rate, 70%.
options.D: Signing authority and rental documentation both need checking; future rent need not always be excluded; probability-weighted income is $4,200, so the probability is 0%.

explanation: Future rental income is not categorically excluded from personal commercial-property loan income assessment. The signed lease, property visit, and LLC's existence do not establish the purported manager's authority to act for the owner. That authority remains unverified, which does not itself prove the lease legally invalid. Under the stipulated policy, income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and documentation passes; otherwise it is $3,000. Partitioning by verified versus unverified authority, the law of total probability gives P(income ≥ $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. A documentation pass without verified authority cannot qualify the rent.

distractor_analysis.reason: It mistakes the signed lease and the LLC's existence for evidence of the signer's authority. Its 70% result counts documentation passes even when authority is unverified, contrary to the policy.

It correctly identifies the authority gap and calculates the documentation-pass rate, 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 70%, but does not integrate the authority requirement into the income-threshold event.

It uses the 60% joint success probability to calculate expected credited income, $3,000 + 0.60 × $2,000 = $4,200. Expected income below the threshold does not imply zero probability of reaching it: the investigation supports $5,000 with probability 60%.

As in the retrieved housing post, the premises and LLC exist and a signed lease is available, but the manager's authority is undocumented. Ask what remains to be verified and calculate the probability that the completed investigation supports qualifying monthly income of at least $4,500. Supply salary of $3,000 and potential future rent of $2,000. Explicitly stipulate a hypothetical bank policy requiring both verified signing authority and a satisfactory rental-income documentation check before crediting that rent. Supply a 75% probability that authority is verified, and documentation-check pass probabilities of 80% if authority is verified and 40% if it is not. Ask whether future rent must always be excluded, and require a total-probability calculation after applying the policy. Do not ask for a jurisdiction-specific enforceability ruling.

answer_plans.plan: Reject categorical exclusion of future rental income. Identify the missing evidence as the purported manager's authority to act for the owner LLC; the signed lease, property visit, and LLC's existence do not resolve that factual gap. Under the stipulated policy, qualifying income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and the documentation check passes; otherwise it is $3,000. Partition by verified versus unverified authority and calculate P(income >= $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. Explain that an unverified lease is not thereby proven legally invalid.

Treat the signed lease and existence of the owner LLC as sufficient evidence of the manager's authority. Ignore the distinct authority-verification requirement and count any documentation-check pass as sufficient, calculating 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 0.70.

Correctly flag the unresolved signing authority and explain that future rent can count. Separately compute the unconditional probability of passing the documentation check as 70%, but never use the authority requirement to determine the probability of meeting the qualifying-income threshold.

Correctly identify both required checks and compute their joint success probability as 60%, but then multiply the $2,000 rent by 60% and classify the borrower solely from $4,200 of probability-weighted income. Incorrectly report a zero probability of meeting the $4,500 threshold, confusing expected income with the probability of crossing a threshold.

legal.necessity: The post provides a signed lease despite the unresolved authority issue, supporting the distinction between having a document and verifying its signer's role.
The signer claims to act for the owner LLC, making authority to rent on the owner's behalf the relevant investigation issue.
The absence of evidence connecting the manager to the LLC supplies the unresolved fact that the hypothetical bank policy requires investigators to verify; it does not establish legal invalidity.

mathematics.necessity: Verified and unverified authority are mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes for structuring the calculation.
The probability of meeting the income threshold must be evaluated within each authority outcome after applying both bank requirements.
The law of total probability combines the conditional threshold probabilities into the overall 60% result.

question: A bank is investigating a personal commercial-property loan. The premises have been visited, the selling owner LLC's existence is confirmed, and an existing lease is signed by a purported manager for the LLC, but no evidence of the manager's authority is available. The borrower's accepted monthly salary is $3,000, and the property could generate $2,000 in future monthly rent. Under a hypothetical bank policy, the full rent counts only if signing authority is verified AND a rental-income documentation check passes; otherwise no rent counts. Authority verification succeeds with probability 75%. The documentation check passes with probability 80% if authority is verified and 40% otherwise. Which assessment correctly addresses future rent, the remaining verification, and the probability that the completed investigation supports monthly income of at least $4,500?

options.A: Future rent need not always be excluded. The lease and LLC's existence establish authority, leaving only the documentation check; the probability is 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 70%.
options.B: Future rent need not always be excluded. Verify the manager's authority and complete the documentation check; the probability is 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 60%.
options.C: Future rent need not always be excluded. Authority remains unverified and the documentation check is required; report its overall pass rate, 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 70%, as the requested probability.
options.D: Future rent need not always be excluded. Both checks remain required and succeed jointly with probability 60%; probability-weighted income is $4,200, so the probability of reaching $4,500 is 0%.

explanation: The financial sample rejects the categorical exclusion of future rental income. The legal sample illustrates that a signed lease, a visit to the premises, and an existing LLC do not resolve whether the purported manager is authorized to act for the owner. That authority remains to be verified; missing proof does not itself establish that the lease is legally invalid. Under the stipulated bank policy, income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and the documentation check passes, and $3,000 otherwise. Partitioning outcomes into verified and unverified authority, the law of total probability gives P(income ≥ $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. A documentation pass without verified authority cannot qualify the rent.

distractor_analysis.reason: It treats a signed lease and the LLC's existence as proof of the signer's authority. Those facts leave the authorization gap unresolved, so documentation passes in the unverified-authority branch cannot count toward qualifying income.

It correctly identifies the unresolved authority issue and correctly calculates the unconditional documentation-pass probability. However, it reports that separate probability without applying both policy requirements to the income-threshold event.

It correctly calculates the joint success probability but incorrectly uses expected income to decide a threshold probability. The $4,200 probability-weighted average does not eliminate the 60% chance of qualifying income being $5,000.

Explicitly stipulate a hypothetical bank policy requiring both verified signing authority and a satisfactory rental-income documentation check before crediting that rent. Supply a 75% probability that authority is verified, and documentation-check pass probabilities of 80% if authority is verified and 40% if it is not. Ask whether future rent must always be excluded, and require a total-probability calculation after applying the policy. Do not ask for a jurisdiction-specific enforceability ruling.

answer_plans.plan: Reject categorical exclusion of future rental income. Identify the missing evidence as the purported manager's authority to act for the owner LLC; the signed lease, property visit, and LLC's existence do not resolve that factual gap. Under the stipulated policy, qualifying income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and the documentation check passes; otherwise it is $3,000. Partition by verified versus unverified authority and calculate P(income >= $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. Explain that an unverified lease is not thereby proven legally invalid.

Treat the signed lease and existence of the owner LLC as sufficient evidence of the manager's authority. Ignore the distinct authority-verification requirement and count any documentation-check pass as sufficient, calculating 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 0.70.

Correctly flag the unresolved signing authority and explain that future rent can count. Separately compute the unconditional probability of passing the documentation check as 70%, but never use the authority requirement to determine the probability of meeting the qualifying-income threshold.

Correctly identify both required checks and compute their joint success probability as 60%, but then multiply the $2,000 rent by 60% and classify the borrower solely from $4,200 of probability-weighted income. Incorrectly report a zero probability of meeting the $4,500 threshold, confusing expected income with the probability of crossing a threshold.

legal.necessity: The post provides a signed lease despite the unresolved authority issue, supporting the distinction between having a document and verifying its signer's role.
The signer claims to act for the owner LLC, making authority to rent on the owner's behalf the relevant investigation issue.
The absence of evidence connecting the manager to the LLC supplies the unresolved fact that the hypothetical bank policy requires investigators to verify; it does not establish legal invalidity.

mathematics.necessity: Verified and unverified authority are mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes for structuring the calculation.
The probability of meeting the income threshold must be evaluated within each authority outcome after applying both bank requirements.
The law of total probability combines the conditional threshold probabilities into the overall 60% result.

question: A bank investigates a personal commercial-property loan. The premises have been visited, the selling owner LLC exists, and an existing lease signed by its purported manager is available, but nothing documents the manager's authority to act for the LLC. The borrower has $3,000 monthly salary and $2,000 potential monthly rent from the purchased property. All other requirements are satisfied. A hypothetical bank policy credits the full rent only if signing authority is verified AND a rental-income documentation check passes; otherwise it credits no rent. Authority verification succeeds with probability 75%. The documentation check passes with probability 80% if authority is verified and 40% otherwise. Which assessment correctly identifies the remaining verification, states whether future rent must always be excluded, and calculates the probability that qualifying monthly income is at least $4,500?

options.A: The lease and LLC's existence establish authority; only the documentation check remains. Future rent need not always be excluded. Probability: 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0.40 = 70%.
options.B: Signing authority and rental documentation remain to be verified. Future rent need not always be excluded. Probability: 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 60%.
options.C: Signing authority and rental documentation remain to be verified. Future rent need not always be excluded. The unconditional documentation-pass probability is 70%, which is the requested probability.
options.D: Signing authority and rental documentation remain to be verified. Future rent need not always be excluded. Both checks succeed with probability 60%, yielding $4,200 probability-weighted income and thus a 0% chance of qualifying.

explanation: Future rental income is not categorically excluded from personal commercial-property loan income assessment. However, the signed lease, property visit, and LLC's existence do not establish the purported manager's authority; that factual gap remains to be checked and does not itself prove the lease legally invalid. Under the stipulated policy, income is $5,000 only when authority is verified and documentation passes, and $3,000 otherwise. Partitioning outcomes into verified and unverified authority gives P(income ≥ $4,500) = 0.75 × 0.80 + 0.25 × 0 = 0.60. Even a successful documentation check cannot qualify the rent when authority remains unverified.

distractor_analysis.reason: It treats possession of a signed lease and confirmation that the LLC exists as proof of the signer's authority. These facts leave the authorization gap unresolved. Its 70% calculation improperly includes documentation passes without verified authority.

It correctly identifies the outstanding checks and correctly computes the unconditional documentation-pass probability, but does not integrate the authority requirement into the threshold event. Passing documentation alone is not sufficient to credit rent.

It correctly finds the 60% joint success probability but substitutes expected income, $3,000 + 0.60 × $2,000 = $4,200, for the distribution of qualifying income. Income is actually $5,000 with probability 60% and $3,000 otherwise, so an expectation below $4,500 does not imply a zero chance of reaching that threshold.

question: During a practice quality inspection, a regulator requests a Chinese CPA firm's confidential memo on its client's merger agreement. The client refuses consent. The MAE clause excludes public health events, including COVID-19, “and the governmental responses thereto (including any COVID-19 Measures),” but counts effects only to the extent materially disproportionate relative to similarly sized industry peers. Two files exist: • Measures.txt: Governmental responses are expressly excluded, subject to that disproportionate-effect qualification. • Unmentioned.txt: Governmental responses are not mentioned. Which response correctly selects and retrieves the memo, applies CPA confidentiality rules, and assesses whether file dumping alone prevents unauthorized use?

options.A: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Withhold it until the client consents. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.B: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. It may be provided for the inspection without client consent; confidentiality toward others remains. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.C: Recognize that the clause expressly excludes governmental responses subject to the qualification, but retrieve Unmentioned.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Provide it without client consent. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.D: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Although inspections generally permit disclosure without consent, withhold this memo because the contractual MAE exclusion also exempts it from inspection disclosure. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.

explanation: Measures.txt accurately describes the express inclusion of pandemic governmental responses in the MAE exclusions and the qualification for materially disproportionate effects. File systems support access by filename and establish a directory entry when a file is created. Under the supplied Chinese CPA confidentiality rule, a member may disclose confidential information and answer regulatory inquiries during a practice quality inspection without obtaining client consent. This permission does not remove confidentiality toward others, and file dumping alone does not ensure protection against unauthorized use.

distractor_analysis.reason: It selects and retrieves the accurate memo and correctly rejects dumping as authorization protection, but overlooks the CPA practice quality inspection exception by requiring client consent.
It states the relevant legal, confidentiality, and file-system facts but fails to connect the legal interpretation to file selection: Unmentioned.txt contradicts the clause.

It incorrectly turns a contractual exclusion from the MAE definition into an exemption from regulatory inspection disclosure. The clause governs MAE treatment, not whether the CPA may provide the memo.

question: During a practice quality inspection of a Chinese CPA firm, a regulator requests the confidential memo correctly interpreting a client's merger agreement. The client refuses consent. The MAE clause excludes public-health events “including COVID-19” and “the governmental responses thereto (including any COVID-19 Measures),” but counts effects only to the extent materially disproportionate to similarly sized industry peers. Two files are available: • Measures.txt: Governmental responses are expressly excluded, subject to that disproportionate-effect qualification. • Silence.txt: Governmental responses are not mentioned. Which response correctly selects and retrieves the memo, applies CPA confidentiality requirements, and assesses whether file dumping alone prevents unauthorized use?

options.A: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation; withhold it until the client consents. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.B: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation; provide it to the inspector without client consent, maintaining confidentiality toward others. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.C: Recognize the qualified exclusion of governmental responses, but retrieve and provide Silence.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Inspection disclosure needs no client consent; file dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.D: Retrieve Measures.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation; although inspections generally permit disclosure without consent, withhold this memo because its subject is excluded from MAE. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.

explanation: Measures.txt accurately describes the express exclusion of pandemic governmental responses, including COVID-19 Measures, and the qualification allowing effects to count only to the extent materially disproportionate to similarly sized industry peers. A file system supports access by filename and establishes a directory entry when a file is created. Under the Chinese CPA confidentiality principle, a member undergoing a practice quality inspection may disclose confidential information and respond to the inspector without obtaining client consent. That permission does not remove confidentiality obligations toward others, and file dumping alone does not ensure protection from unauthorized use.

distractor_analysis.reason: It selects the accurate memo and correctly describes file handling, but overlooks the CPA practice quality inspection exception by requiring client consent.

It states the relevant contract interpretation, disclosure permission, and file-system facts, but fails to connect the interpretation to file selection: Silence.txt contradicts the clause and does not answer the regulator's request correctly.

It incorrectly turns a contractual MAE exclusion into a restriction on regulatory disclosure. The exclusion concerns how effects are assessed under the merger agreement, not whether the CPA may provide the memo during a practice quality inspection.

question: During a Chinese CPA firm's practice quality inspection, a regulator requests the confidential memo correctly interpreting a client's merger agreement. The client refuses consent. The MAE clause excludes “any national or global outbreak of illness or other national or global public health event (including COVID-19) and the governmental responses thereto (including any COVID-19 Measures).” This exclusion applies only insofar as effects are not materially disproportionate relative to similarly sized industry peers; effects may count only to that disproportionate extent. Two files are available: • scope.txt: Governmental responses are expressly excluded, subject to the disproportionate-effect qualification. • silence.txt: The clause does not mention pandemic governmental measures. Which workflow correctly selects the requested memo, applies CPA confidentiality, identifies filename access and the record established at file creation, and assesses whether file dumping alone prevents unauthorized use?

options.A: Retrieve scope.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Its interpretation is correct, but withhold it until the client consents. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.B: Retrieve scope.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Provide it to the inspector without client consent while preserving confidentiality toward others. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.C: Recognize that governmental responses are expressly excluded subject to disproportionate effects, but retrieve and provide silence.txt. Inspection disclosure needs no client consent; use filename access and its directory entry established at creation. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.
options.D: Retrieve scope.txt by filename using its directory entry established at creation. Although inspection disclosure generally needs no client consent, withhold this memo because the contractual MAE exclusion also excludes it from inspection disclosure. File dumping alone does not prevent unauthorized use.

explanation: The clause expressly includes pandemic governmental responses, including COVID-19 Measures, within its MAE exclusions, but allows effects to count to the extent they are materially disproportionate relative to similarly sized industry peers. Thus scope.txt is the requested accurate memo. Under the Chinese CPA confidentiality principle, a member may disclose confidential information and respond to inquiries during a practice quality inspection without obtaining client consent. This permission does not eliminate confidentiality toward others. The file system supports access by filename and establishes a directory entry when a file is created. File dumping alone does not ensure protection against unauthorized users.

distractor_analysis.reason: It selects the legally accurate memo and correctly describes file access and dumping, but overlooks the CPA practice quality inspection exception by requiring client consent.

It states the relevant contract interpretation, inspection permission, and file-system facts, but fails to connect the interpretation to file selection: silence.txt contradicts the clause and is not the requested accurate memo.

It wrongly transfers a contractual exclusion from the MAE definition into an exemption from regulatory inspection disclosure. The clause governs which effects count toward MAE, not whether the CPA may disclose the memo to a practice quality inspector.
